This is **"Hydra: Sequentially-Dependent Draft Heads for Medusa Decoding"** (arXiv:2402.05109), and it was published at COLM 2024.

**Publication details**
- **Authors:** Zachary Ankner, Rishab Parthasarathy, Aniruddha Nrusimha, Christopher Rinard, Jonathan Ragan-Kelley, William Brandon. They are affiliated with MIT and MosaicML.
- **Dates:** Submitted on 7 Feb 2024 (v1), last revised 7 Oct 2024 (this version, v2)
- **Venue:** The v2 PDF says it was published as a conference paper at COLM 2024. There is also an OpenReview page (openreview.net/forum?id=FbhjirzvJG).

**Background**
- In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes candidate continuations of the input sequence that are then verified in parallel by the base model.
- Medusa builds the draft model as a collection of lightweight heads, called draft heads, that operate on the base model's hidden states. Medusa's authors choose to use a single-layer MLP with a residual connection for each head.
- The problem the paper targets: all existing draft heads have been sequentially independent, meaning that they speculate tokens in the candidate continuation independently of any preceding tokens in the candidate continuation.

**What Hydra changes**
- Hydra heads are a sequentially-dependent drop-in replacement for standard draft heads that significantly improves the accuracy of draft head speculation.
- Each Hydra head uses both the base model's hidden state up to time t as well as the input embeddings of the tokens sampled by previous Hydra heads.
- The authors also tested different training objectives and architectures, ending up with a tuned recipe called Hydra++. It improves decoding throughput by up to 1.31x and 2.70x compared to Medusa decoding and autoregressive de-coding respectively.

**Setup and results**
- Training used the ShareGPT dataset (ShareGPT, 2023), a collection of multi-turn conversations, on 8× NVIDIA A100-80GB GPUs. Evaluation was performed on MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), a multi-turn conversation benchmark.
- Compared with standard autoregressive decoding, basic Hydra heads achieve a 2.36×, 2.17×, and 2.15× improvement in throughput as compared to autoregressive decoding for the 7B, 13B, and 33B parameter base models respectively. Compared with Medusa, that works out to 1.11×, 1.10×, and 1.11× for the same model sizes.
- Across all base model sizes evaluated, Hydra achieves higher average acceptance lengths than Medusa, and Hydra++ achieves higher acceptance lengths than Hydra. In both cases this leads to large throughput gains.

The code is public; the arXiv abstract page links to it.

The paper is arXiv 2406.13170, called **Amphista**.

**Titles and versions**
- The first version came out in June 2024 under the title "Amphista: Accelerate LLM Inference with Bi-directional Multiple Drafting Heads in a Non-autoregressive Style." The authors describe it as a speculative decoding algorithm that follows a non-autoregressive decoding approach.
- Version 2 (October 2024) was renamed "Amphista: Bi-directional Multi-head Decoding for Accelerating LLM Inference".
- It was later published at NAACL 2025 (the long paper is in the ACL Anthology).

**The problem it addresses**
LLMs generate text one token at a time. This gives little room for parallel work during inference and makes it slow, especially when parallel hardware and memory bandwidth aren't fully used. Amphista builds on Medusa, which drafts several future tokens at once using separate "heads." The authors found that each independent Medusa head predicts with fairly low accuracy, and accuracy gets worse for each later head, which hurts speedup.

**What Amphista changes**
1. **Auto-embedding Block:** A bi-directional Transformer Encoder with positional encoding. It lets each head attend to the others so they predict together, which makes drafts more accurate.
2. **Staged Adaptation Layers:** A group of causal Transformer Decoder layers on top of the target model. They adjust the model's hidden states and the sampled token in two stages, so the features carry more context and can support predicting several tokens, not just the next one.

**Results**
- On MT-Bench with Vicuna 33B, Amphista runs up to 2.75× faster than normal autoregressive decoding and 1.40× faster than Medusa, measured in wall-clock time.
- Hydra, which also uses multiple drafting heads but drafts autoregressively, was the main baseline. The authors compared against its best version, Hydra++, and used vicuna-68m as the draft model for standard speculative decoding. All experiments ran on A100 40G GPUs.
- Speculative decoding is lossless: thanks to rejection sampling, the output quality matches the target model's.

- arXiv abstract: arxiv.org/abs/2406.13170
- Full text (HTML): arxiv.org/html/2406.13170v2
- NAACL version: aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.450.pdf

**The problem it addresses**
LLMs generate text one token at a time. This gives little room for parallel work during inference and makes it slow, especially when parallel hardware and memory bandwidth aren't fully used. Amphista builds on Medusa, which drafts several future tokens at once using separate "heads." The authors found that each independent Medusa head predicts with fairly low accuracy, and accuracy gets worse for each later head, which hurts speedup.

**What Amphista changes**
1. **Auto-embedding Block:** A bi-directional Transformer Encoder with positional encoding. It lets each head attend to the others so they predict together, which makes drafts more accurate.
2. **Staged Adaptation Layers:** A group of causal Transformer Decoder layers on top of the target model. They adjust the model's hidden states and the sampled token in two stages, so the features carry more context and can support predicting several tokens, not just the next one.

**Results**
- On MT-Bench with Vicuna 33B, Amphista runs up to 2.75× faster than normal autoregressive decoding and 1.40× faster than Medusa, measured in wall-clock time.
- Hydra, which also uses multiple drafting heads but drafts autoregressively, was the main baseline. The authors compared against its best version, Hydra++, and used vicuna-68m as the draft model for standard speculative decoding. All experiments ran on A100 40G GPUs.
- Speculative decoding is lossless: thanks to rejection sampling, the output quality matches the target model's.

The authors propose a new model for multi-token prediction in transformers, aiming to enhance sampling efficiency without compromising accuracy. Earlier methods used several heads to predict upcoming tokens. The authors show that this approach is the same as a rank-1 canonical tensor decomposition. By generalizing it to a rank-r canonical probability decomposition, they develop an improved model that predicts multiple tokens simultaneously.

- **Why rank-1 falls short:** The rank-1 version treats future tokens as independent of each other. The paper calls this a crude approximation that may limit token acceptance rates due to its disregard for token interdependencies.

- The ability to fine-tune only the prediction head of the model while maintaining competitive performance highlights the flexibility of the approach.

I found the paper you were looking for. It's on arXiv and was published at NeurIPS 2024.

**Paper details**
- **arXiv ID:** 2412.00061. Zhuofan Wen submitted v1 on Mon, 25 Nov 2024.
- **Authors and venue:** Wen, Zhuofan and Gui, Shangtong and Feng, Yang, in The Thirty-eighth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024). It was presented as a poster, and the paper also appears in the NeurIPS proceedings and the ACM Digital Library.
- **Code:** It's on GitHub at ZhuofanWen/CTC-drafter, which includes training and evaluation. This repo is modified from Medusa and Eagle.

**The problem it addresses**
In speculative decoding, the final inference speed is decided by the decoding speed of the draft model and the acceptance rate of the draft provided by the draft model. Currently the widely used draft models usually generate draft tokens for the next several positions in a non-autoregressive way without considering the correlations between draft tokens. Therefore, it has a high decoding speed but an unsatisfactory acceptance rate.

**How it works**
- The authors propose a CTC-based draft model which strengthens the correlations between draft tokens during the draft phase, thereby generating higher-quality draft candidate sequences. They say it is the first to apply the CTC algorithm within the speculative decoding domain.
- Architecture: the model inserts a transformer layer on top of the base LLM's hidden states and trains it with a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) loss on distilled labels from the base model.
- Inference: it selects top-k tokens at each of several future positions, combines them into a token tree, removes blank symbols and consecutive duplicate tokens through a CTC Transform Module, and masks the removed positions in the attention map so that parallel verification sees only the surviving sequence.

**Results**
- On MT-bench, CTC-drafter achieves better draft quality compared to other works, with more than three tokens accepted per decoding step. Higher predicting accuracy enables CTC-drafter to achieve a speedup ratio of more than 2×, outperforming Medusa and Hydra on all types of base model.
- Across Vicuna-7B/13B/33B and LLaMA-2-Chat on MT-bench and GSM8K, it reports between 3.4 and 3.6 accepted tokens per decoding step and speedups of 2.2x to 2.8x over vanilla autoregressive decoding.
- The extra drafting work has a cost: replacing the original Medusa head with a transformer layer increased the draft model's share of time from 3.71% to 14.93%, and the CTC transform accounts for an extra 5.36% of overall decoding time.
- Speedups get smaller on bigger models. This is attributed to the growing ability gap between the draft module and the larger base models.

**Criticism from one review**
An unofficial review on Pith raised two concerns. First, it argues that the claim that the improvement comes from CTC-induced correlations among draft tokens isn't backed by the paper's own inference procedure or ablation design. Second, the reported speedup over Hydra is also weakened by the fact that Hydra's numbers are taken from the original paper rather than measured in the same setup.

**Links**

- NeurIPS PDF: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/a79054a9da91d73ed3cb1a9e87d7cd2d-Paper-Conference.pdf

**Title:** Accelerating Speculative Diffusions via Block Verification (arXiv:2606.13426, cs.LG / stat.ML)

**Authors:** Alexander Soen, Hisham Husain, Valentin De Bortoli, Arnaud Doucet

**Date:** Submitted 11 June 2026 (v1)

**Abstract (summary):** In LLMs, speculative decoding has a draft model propose tokens, and an accept/reject step keeps outputs faithful to the target distribution. Carrying this over to continuous diffusions is hard because speculative sampling needs draws from a residual distribution. That is easy with discrete tokens but difficult in continuous space. Earlier diffusion versions either sample inefficiently or use a different scheme. The authors propose a new way to run the original speculative sampling mechanism efficiently for diffusion models. This lets them bring block verification from LLMs to diffusions, which "provably improves the acceptance rate of drafts." They also formalize and analyze the "Free Drafter," a training-free, self-speculative heuristic drafter. With block verification, it gives "up to a 6.3% speedup over existing speculative methods," with no extra training and little overhead beyond the parallel verification pass.

**Which framing?** It is about **speculative decoding for diffusion models**. The diffusion model is the target being accelerated. It is not about diffusion drafters for autoregressive targets. Block verification is borrowed from LLM work and applied to continuous diffusions. The method keeps output matching the target distribution, so it is lossless in that sense.

**Trees?** The page never mentions tree-based drafting or verification. It only discusses block verification and the self-speculative Free Drafter.

The paper is **arXiv:2510.04147**, "Self Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models," posted around October 5, 2025.

**What it does**
- **The problem:** Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) can decode many tokens at once, but the generation results of current parallel decoding methods deviate from stepwise decoding, introducing potential performance degradation, which limits their practical deployment.
- **The method:** SSD is a lossless inference acceleration method that leverages the dLLM itself as both speculative decoding drafter and verifier without auxiliary modules. The model generates predictions for multiple positions, then verifies them through hierarchical verification trees in a single forward pass.
- **How drafting works:** At the start of inference and after each verification round, the dLLM runs a single forward pass to produce draft tokens and confidence scores for all masked positions. It then selects up to N positions for verification, following the semi-autoregressive block constraints of dLLMs.

**How the verification tree works**
- Each node in the tree is a sequence state with one more accepted token than its parent. A child node is only valid if its parent's token exactly matches what stepwise generation would produce.
- For draft length N, the greedy strategy builds a verification batch of size N + 1. The root node is the starting state with no verified draft tokens, and the leaf node is the state where all N draft tokens are accepted. Under the greedy strategy, every non-leaf node has only one child.
- If verification fails at a node, all tokens after that point are rejected.

**Results**
- Experiments on five dLLMs across four benchmarks show up to 3.46× speedup while keeping the generated output identical.

**Limitations**
- Acceptance rate is limited because only top-1 confidence tokens are drafted. Checking the top 2 candidates improves it by only 5–7%, and k-ary trees grow the batch size exponentially (Θ(k^N)), which makes inference memory-bound and cancels out the speedup.
- A common failure is out-of-order generation: the draft has the correct tokens but in a different order than step-by-step decoding. A "mix-order" strategy cuts another 2.5%–3.1% of steps but needs 50%–67% larger verification batches, so the authors keep the greedy strategy.

The paper is at arxiv.org/abs/2510.04147, with an HTML version, a Hugging Face paper page and an alphaXiv discussion page.

I found the paper. Here's a summary:

**Paper:** SpecDiff-2: Scaling Diffusion Drafter Alignment For Faster Speculative Decoding (arXiv:2511.00606). The authors are Jameson Sandler, Jacob K. Christopher, Thomas Hartvigsen and Ferdinando Fioretto. It was also given an oral presentation at the Conference on Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 2026.

**The problem it tackles:** According to the authors, speculative decoding is held back by two bottlenecks: (1) the autoregressive dependency during drafting which limits parallelism, and (2) frequent rejections of draft tokens caused by misalignment between the draft and verify models. To fix the first, it uses discrete diffusion as a non-autoregressive drafter. To fix the second, it develops new ways to calibrate the diffusion drafter against the autoregressive verifier.

**Two main parts:** SpecDiff-2 uses a train-time (de-facto, fine-tuning) procedure called streak-distillation, that improves proposer alignment with the verifier by targeting theoretical acceleration, and a test-time acceptance mechanism, called self-selection acceptance, that uses the verifier to select drafts that maximize throughput.

**How self-selection works:** For prefix s and draft of size γ, the drafter generates marginals q1, ..., qγ, and expands them into K discrete drafts of length γ via sampling. In short, diffusion models can produce several candidate drafts at little extra cost, so SpecDiff-2 generates K drafts at once. The verifier then scores them and picks the one most likely to give the longest accepted sequence. The paper also tests how speedup grows with the number of parallel drafts K when self-selection is used. These tests used Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct on Math500 prompts (out of distribution).

**Why streak-distillation:** Standard distillation tends to cause a "front-loading" effect in block-based drafting, where accuracy drops sharply as the sequence progresses. Streak-distillation significantly improves the position-wise acceptance rate compared to base and standard AR-distillation methods, achieving up to a 3.2× improvement at larger distances from the prefix.

**Results:** SpecDiff-2 achieves a new state-of-the-art across reasoning, coding, and mathematical benchmarks, improving tokens-per-second by up to an average of +55% over previous baselines and obtaining up to 5.5× average speed-up over standard decoding, without any loss of accuracy. The benchmarks include Math500 (mathematical reasoning), HumanEval (code generation), and GPQA (science questions). The aligned drafter also outperforms the base SpecDiff drafter by over 40%. All evaluations keep the output lossless (identical to the verifier model) across all methods.

- PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.00606
- HTML (v2): https://arxiv.org/html/2511.00606v2
- MLSys 2026 slides: https://mlsys.org/media/mlsys-2026/Slides/3755.pdf

I found the paper. Here's an overview of **BiTA: Bi-Directional Tuning for Lossless Acceleration in Large Language Models** (arXiv:2401.12522).

**Basic details**
- **Authors:** Feng Lin, Hanling Yi, Hongbin Li, Yifan Yang, Xiaotian Yu, Guangming Lu and Rong Xiao. The first version went up on 23 Jan 2024 and was revised on 25 Jan 2024 (v2). 
- **Affiliations:** Intellifusion Inc. and Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen. 
- **Journal version:** The paper later appeared in *Expert Systems with Applications* (ScienceDirect, 2025). That version calls BiTA "an innovative speculative decoding method that expedites LLMs through streamlined semi-autoregressive generation and draft verification." The code is at https://github.com/linfeng93/BiTA.

**What problem it solves**
LLMs normally generate text one token at a time (autoregressively). This leads to high memory bandwidth demand and consequently extended latency.

**How it works**
BiTA has two core parts:

1. **Bi-directional tuning with prompt tokens:** Inspired by the concept of prompt tuning, the authors add a parameter-efficient design called bi-directional tuning that lets LLMs do semi-autoregressive generation. It adds both prompt tokens and mask tokens so the model can predict several future tokens, not just the next one. The authors describe these as learnable prefix and suffix embeddings in the token sequence.
2. **Tree-based decoding:** Using efficient tree-based decoding, the model generates draft candidates and verifies them in parallel. Under greedy sampling, the outputs are identical to normal autoregressive generation. A tree-based attention mechanism lets generation and verification happen together in a single forward pass, so no extra validation steps or external verification models are needed.

**Results**
- With BiTA, LLaMA-2-70B-Chat runs 2.7× faster on the MT-Bench benchmark.
- According to a third-party summary on Emergent Mind, it adds as few as 0.01% additional parameters. Across different LLMs and tasks, speedups ranged from 2.1× to 3.3×, and the gains were larger for bigger models.
- BiTA works as a lightweight plug-in module. It speeds up existing LLMs without extra assistant models or significant extra memory. The authors report that it beats state-of-the-art acceleration techniques.

**How it compares to standard speculative decoding**
The journal version says BiTA turns an off-the-shelf LLM into its own draft model. This removes the need for an external draft generator and avoids poor drafts from an unsuitable draft model.

The paper is arXiv 2404.12022, released in April 2024. Tree attention is how its method checks draft tokens so the final output is exactly what normal decoding would produce.

**The main idea: hidden transfer**
The paper proposes a parallel decoding method called hidden transfer, which decodes multiple successive tokens simultaneously in a single forward pass. It does this by transferring the intermediate hidden states of the previous context to the pseudo hidden states of the future tokens to be generated. Those "pseudo" states then go through the rest of the model's layers, which gives them more context and makes the predictions more accurate. In practice, at a specific intermediate layer (e.g., layer 15 of a 32-layer model), a trainable linear projection maps the current token's hidden state into "pseudo" hidden states for the next $k$ tokens. During training, KL-divergence is used as the supervised signal, which minimizes the distribution between tokens predicted by the pseudo hidden states and the real ones.

**How tree attention is used**
- The authors use the tree attention mechanism (Cai et al., 2023; Miao et al., 2023; Spector and Re, 2023) to simultaneously perform the token prediction and token verification to ensure the lossless generation of the method.
- Step by step: multiple sequence candidates are merged into a tree structure by their common ancestors. The tree is then flattened into a sequence with an attention mask that keeps their order, and the whole sequence is sent into the LLM to verify the candidates and generate the new candidates at the same time.
- Draft tokens belonging to different steps form a tree structure according to their order. The tree attention mechanism transforms this hierarchical tree into a linear sequence while preserving the original positional indices of each token.
- One summary explains that tokens are accepted only if the model's original output head agrees with the drafted sequence.

**Results**
- In terms of acceleration metrics, the method outperforms all the single-model acceleration techniques, including Medusa and Self-Speculative decoding.
- According to a third-party summary, Hidden Transfer achieved a 2.275x speedup for LLaMA-2-13B and 2.135x for LLaMA-2-7B on the Gsm8k benchmark.
- The motivation is that GPUs sit partly idle during normal one-token-at-a-time decoding. The authors measured that with a KV cache, increasing the length of the input sequence within a certain range does not increase forward-propagation time.

**Limitations and future work on tree attention**
The authors write that in the verification stage they simply used vanilla tree attention without specific optimization. They note that the structural choices of tree attention significantly impact the generation speed. Also, the approach requires expanding the input sequence during both training and inference, which may increase computational resource requirements.

**Related work**
A later paper, "Acceleration Multiple Heads Decoding for LLM via Dynamic Tree Attention" (arXiv 2502.05947), takes up this question for Medusa. It replaces the fixed tree attention with dynamic tree attention on multiple head decoding, specifically in the context of MEDUSA.

- **Title:** Acceleration Multiple Heads Decoding for LLM via Dynamic Tree Attention
- **Author:** Zhendong Zhang (sole author)
- **Date:** Submitted 9 February 2025 (v1)
- **Venue:** An arXiv preprint (arXiv:2502.05947). Its primary category is cs.CV, with a cross-listing in cs.CL. The page names no conference or journal. It is licensed CC BY 4.0.

**Abstract (paraphrased)**
Multiple-heads decoding speeds up LLM inference by predicting several upcoming tokens at once. It then checks candidate sequences in parallel using tree attention "with a fixed structure." This work swaps that fixed tree for a dynamic one within MEDUSA. It proposes "a simple and low complexity strategy to generate candidates and construct the dynamic tree structure." Early experiments show better decoding efficiency "while maintaining the generation quality." The author says this points to room for improving how multi-head decoding generates candidates.

**Tree construction and budgeting**
The page doesn't answer either question. It only says candidates and the dynamic tree come from a "simple and low complexity strategy." It does not say:
- whether candidates come from a Cartesian product of the heads' per-position marginals, from top-k per head, or from some other method;
- whether the tree size is fixed, budgeted, or adaptive.

To find out, you'd need the full text, which is available as a PDF, an HTML version, or TeX source on arXiv.

content.content:
**Tree vs. chain:** The paper only reports chain drafting. Table 10 says: "All experiments use chain drafting and are measured on 1 H200 GPU." It never evaluates tree verification for P-EAGLE.

Every mention of "tree" refers to other work:
- Related Work, on Falcon: "through dependency-aware training and a custom decoding tree"
- Falcon's reference title: "custom-designed decoding tree"
- SpecInfer's reference title: "tree-based speculative inference and verification"

**vLLM integration:** The paper says only that the authors "implement P-EAGLE's parallel drafting in vLLM." It gives no `parallel_drafting` flag, no configuration option names and no vLLM version.

**Concurrency and batch size:**
- **Inference:** Table 10 reports throughput (output tokens per second) at concurrency C=2 and C=4, for speculation depths K=3, 5 and 7.
- **Best speedup:** up to "1.36× speedup at concurrency C=2."
- **At C=4:** gains hold for 20B (1.24×–1.27×) but shrink for the larger models (1.03×–1.11×). The paper attributes this to verification becoming the bottleneck, noting that for MoE models "expert routing overhead scales with batch size."
- **Training:** batch size 8 with micro-batch size 1, using 8-step gradient accumulation. Appendix A, for the ParallelSpec and PARD comparison, uses a global batch size of 64.
- **Data loading:** the Table 2 timing was measured on 128 examples.

**AMD/ROCm:** Neither is mentioned. All hardware is NVIDIA: 8×H200 for training and 1 H200 for the vLLM benchmarks.

input.prompt: Explain precisely how candidates are generated and the dynamic tree is constructed from the MEDUSA heads' per-position distributions: is it the top-N candidates of the Cartesian product of per-head marginals (joint probability = product of marginals)? Is the number of candidates/tree size fixed (budget)? Quote the key equations/sentences.

toolu_01YDzRxcmRr4okgqp7RZmdMx.prompt: Explain precisely how candidates are generated and the dynamic tree is constructed from the MEDUSA heads' per-position distributions: is it the top-N candidates of the Cartesian product of per-head marginals (joint probability = product of marginals)? Is the number of candidates/tree size fixed (budget)? Quote the key equations/sentences.

content.content:
**Yes. The candidates are the top-n of a Cartesian product of per-head marginals, and the tree size is a fixed budget of n.**

**1. Joint probability is the product of marginals**

The true joint distribution isn't available, so the paper approximates it "using the Cartesian product of marginal distributions, which is provided by MEDUSA heads." With pᵢ⁽ᵏ⁾ as the i-th top prediction of head k, Eq. (1) is:

"P(i₁,i₂,…,i_k) = ∏_{j=1}^{k} p_{i_j}^{(j)}"

**2. Candidate space**

Only the top-m tokens of each head are kept. The authors note "there are ∑_{k=1}^{K} m^k possible candidates." That count covers every prefix length from 1 to K, not just full-depth paths.

**3. Top-n selection (Algorithm 1)**

The goal is to "select top-n candidates with the highest probability," done with a priority queue:
- **Start:** add an entry (P[1,i], i, 1) for each of head 1's top-m tokens. Each entry is (probability, index, depth).
- **For each head k = 2…K:**
  - Create a queue Q capped at n entries.
  - Re-push every existing entry.
  - For each entry at depth k−1, also push its m children: (p·P[k,i], idx×m+i, k).
- **After each level:** keep only Q's survivors as the new set S.

Cost is "O(Knm log n)," with "K=4, n=64, m=32" taken from the MEDUSA paper.

**4. Why the result is a valid tree**

Eq. (2) shows a child's probability can't exceed its parent's: "P(i₁,…,i_k)=P(i₁,…,i_{k−1})P(i_k) ≤ P(i₁,…,i_{k−1})." So "if candidate (i₁,i₂,…i_k) is selected, then it's parent… is also selected."

**5. Buffers**

From the selected nodes the method builds "the position embedding and attention mask," at a cost of "O(Kn)."

**Is the size fixed?**

Yes, n = 64 nodes, enforced by the size-capped queue. What changes with context is the tree's shape (branching and depth per node). The paper says it "can adapt to context dependencies" while sharing "common parts with the fixed tree structure."

**Caveats**
- The rendered algorithm line "S←set(CLOSE Q)" looks like a conversion artifact; it most likely means S ← set(Q).
- The independence assumption is acknowledged as a limitation that the authors plan to improve.
- The dynamic version raises tokens per inference but runs "approximately 10% slower than MEDUSA" in tokens per second, which they attribute to unoptimized code.

42910 open not-merged 2026-05-18  | [Feature]: Support DDTree speculative decoding | zzl-7

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40809
Add **DDTree** (Diffusion Draft Tree) speculative decoding, implementing the draft-tree construction algorithm from [arXiv:2604.12989](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12989) ("Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Block Diffusion Draft Trees", Ringel & Romano).

DDTree extends the existing DFlash proposer with a dynamic, per-request best-first draft tree instead of a flat greedy sequence. Each proposal step:

1. Runs the DFlash draft model to get per-position logits.
2. Builds an independent draft tree per request via a best-first heap (`build_ddtree_tree`), selecting the `budget` most-probable token paths.
3. Pushes a per-batch `[batch, N+1, N+1]` ancestor-only attention mask to the `TreeAttentionMetadataBuilder` so the target model verifies the full tree in a single forward pass.
4. Uses depth-based RoPE positions (siblings at the same depth share a position ID) so attention correctly treats siblings as alternatives for the same output slot.

Tree verification (`ddtree_verify`) traces the longest accepted path through each request's tree using the target model's greedy predictions.

New config: `speculative_config.method = "ddtree"` with `attention_config.backend = "TREE_ATTN"` required.

# Test Plan

**Model:** `nm-testing/dflash-qwen3-8b-speculators` (Qwen3-8B + DFlash draft)  
**Dataset:** ShareGPT (200 prompts) | **budget:** 64 | `--max-num-seqs 16` | `--max-model-len 4096` | `--enforce-eager`  
**GPU:** NVIDIA RTX 5090 Laptop (24 GiB)

| method | tok/s | req/s | acc\_len | acc\_rate |
|--------|-------|-------|----------|-----------|
| dflash | 130.4 | 0.59  | 2.318    | 0.021     |
| ddtree | 179.7 | 0.81  | 3.406    | 0.038     |

DDTree vs DFlash: acceptance\_len **+1.089** · throughput **+49.3 tok/s (+37.8%)**

> Note: budget=64 is required for meaningful tree branching. At budget=8 the tree is nearly as shallow as a flat chain and gains are modest. `--max-num-seqs 16` is needed to avoid 5090 OOM at this budget/vocab size (Qwen3 vocab ≈ 152k). Extra test with better GPU is needed 

```
.venv/bin/python benchmark_ddtree_sharegpt.py \
    --model nm-testing/dflash-qwen3-8b-speculators \
    --dataset-path /tmp/sharegpt.json \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --num-speculative-tokens 64 \
    --num-prompts 200 \
    --enforce-eager \
    --max-model-len 4096 \
    --max-num-seqs 16 \
    --methods dflash ddtree

```

42910 open not-merged 2026-05-18  | [Feature]: Support DDTree speculative decoding | zzl-7

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40809
Add **DDTree** (Diffusion Draft Tree) speculative decoding, implementing the draft-tree construction algorithm from [arXiv:2604.12989](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12989) ("Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Block Diffusion Draft Trees", Ringel & Romano).

DDTree extends the existing DFlash proposer with a dynamic, per-request best-first draft tree instead of a flat greedy sequence. Each proposal step:

1. Runs the DFlash draft model to get per-position logits.
2. Builds an independent draft tree per request via a best-first heap (`build_ddtree_tree`), selecting the `budget` most-probable token paths.
3. Pushes a per-batch `[batch, N+1, N+1]` ancestor-only attention mask to the `TreeAttentionMetadataBuilder` so the target model verifies the full tree in a single forward pass.
4. Uses depth-based RoPE positions (siblings at the same depth share a position ID) so attention correctly treats siblings as alternatives for the same output slot.

Tree verification (`ddtree_verify`) traces the longest accepted path through each request's tree using the target model's greedy predictions.

New config: `speculative_config.method = "ddtree"` with `attention_config.backend = "TREE_ATTN"` required.

# Test Plan

**Model:** `nm-testing/dflash-qwen3-8b-speculators` (Qwen3-8B + DFlash draft)  
**Dataset:** ShareGPT (200 prompts) | **budget:** 64 | `--max-num-seqs 16` | `--max-model-len 4096` | `--enforce-eager`

|--------|-------|-------|----------|-----------|
| dflash | 130.4 | 0.59  | 2.318    | 0.021     |
| ddtree | 179.7 | 0.81  | 3.406    | 0.038     |

content.content:
--- liranringel 2026-05-21
An author of DDTree here. Excited to see DDTree being implemented in vLLM. Great work on the implementation and speedups!

Just to add some context that may not have been clear enough in our paper: DDTree is not tied to DFlash specifically. It can be implemented for any draft model that outputs marginal per-position distributions over a block of future tokens. This includes DFlash, but also [PARD](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/speculative_decoding/parallel_draft_model/), [P-EAGLE](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-03-13-p-eagle), [Medusa](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/api/vllm/model_executor/models/medusa/), etc.

Since DFlash is currently one of the strongest parallel drafter families with checkpoints trained for many open-weight target models, it is definitely a good starting point to support it first. I also think the current API direction is the right future-proof approach: exposing DDTree with `"method": "ddtree"`, while allowing the actual parallel drafter to be selected independently with `"model": "<drafter>"`. This should make it easier to support other block/parallel drafters later.

--- avisual 2026-05-27
Tested this on DGX Spark (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121a, Blackwell, 128GB unified memory, aarch64) — May 27, 2026. Ran your exact benchmark command — 100 ShareGPT prompts (scaled from 200 for time), `nm-testing/dflash-qwen3-8b-speculators` drafter + `Qwen/Qwen3-8B` target, `--num-speculative-tokens 64 --max-num-seqs 16 --max-model-len 4096 --enforce-eager`, comparing `method=dflash` vs `method=dflash_ddtree` with `ddtree_budget=64`.

| Mode | Wall clock | Aggregate tok/s | Median tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| dflash | 1085.0s | **19.8** | 19.6 |
| dflash_ddtree | 1082.2s | **19.8** | 19.5 |

No measurable speedup. Outputs byte-identical on the 3 prompts I spot-checked (temperature=0 greedy, expected).

Likely culprit: **`--enforce-eager` is disproportionately punishing on Spark's ARM cores.** Our absolute throughput (19.8 tok/s) is ~6–9× lower than your RTX 5090 Laptop's 130.4 tok/s — almost certainly from CPU-side kernel launch overhead dominating without CUDA graphs. Whatever tree-branching advantage DDTree provides is swamped by per-step launch cost on this hardware.

If/when the dynamic-shape issues with tree attention can be reconciled with CUDA graph capture, I'd be happy to re-run on Spark — benchmark infrastructure is in place.

Output correctness on pure-transformer Qwen3-8B looks clean — no quality regressions vs DFlash. (Separately tested on Qwen3.6-27B hybrid via AEON-7's `vllm-aeon-ultimate-ddtree:qwen36-v5-m53-experimental` container in `ddtree-full` mode and saw GDN replay corruption — `self.head = self.head.next` references on LRU code and syntax errors in bug-fix outputs — but that's their experimental wrapper, separate from this PR. The PR's pure-transformer path is solid as far as I can tell.)


--- benchislett 2026-05-27
I do not think we are ready to support/maintain tree drafting right now. I won't close the PR, but please keep it as a draft. It will be a while before tree attention is re-introduced (if at all).

--- rmagur1203 2026-09-02
Sharing measurements from an independent implementation, in case they help
with the "is tree drafting worth maintaining" question.

- Repo: https://github.com/rmagur1203/vllm-ddtree (branch `ddtree-multireq`)
- Findings (English): [`docs/DDTREE-FINDINGS-EN.md`](https://github.com/rmagur1203/vllm-ddtree/blob/ddtree-multireq/docs/DDTREE-FINDINGS-EN.md)
  — verdict matrix, methodology, cost accounting, everything that broke along
  the way and how it was fixed, and the parts reusable regardless of DDTree.

Hardware is 2× RTX A6000 (not 5090), and we didn't test your exact
8B + DFlash pairing, so nothing below directly contradicts your number.
Where it overlaps, it's the measurement method rather than the result.

### On @avisual's "no measurable speedup under eager"

There's a mechanism for that, and it's worse than neutral. Eager execution is
launch-bound, so its GPU idle time absorbs the tree's extra GPU work. Enabling
CUDA graphs removes that slack and the overhead becomes visible. Same config
(Qwen3.5-4B GDN hybrid + DFlash, batch 1, greedy):

| | flat chain | DDTree |
|---|---|---|
| `enforce_eager=True` | 70.9 tok/s | 70.7 — no difference |
| CUDA graph | **144.9** tok/s | **99.1 (−31.6%)** |

Both arms took **the same number of steps (34)** — the tree bought no extra
acceptance at all there, only cost. Per-layer profiling hooks push in the same
direction (~10%). We reported a win for this configuration once and withdrew
it after re-measuring this way.

So I'd suggest re-running the +37.8% with `enforce_eager=False`, no
instrumentation, and counting `execute_model` calls directly so that
acceptance gain and per-step cost are separated. Also worth checking against
vLLM's *default* sampling: with `--generation-config` unset it takes
`temperature/top_k/top_p` from the model's `generation_config.json`
(1.0 / 20 / 0.95 for Qwen3.8), and a `temperature=0` benchmark doesn't
represent that traffic.

### What we tested, and where each one landed

Every drafter type we had — none, n-gram prompt lookup, block-diffusion
(DFlash / DFlash2), autoregressive draft head (EAGLE3) — on targets from 0.6B
to 27B, pure-attention and GDN-hybrid, batch 1–16, greedy and sampled.
DDTree vs. *the same drafter running a flat chain at the same budget*:

| target | drafter | batch | vs chain | what decided it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-0.6B (pure attn) | n-gram | 1 | 0.95x | fewer steps (184 vs 193) but per-step cost not covered; on a 2.7 ms/step model even the chain loses to no-spec |
| Qwen3.5-4B (GDN hybrid) | DFlash | 1 | 0.68x | same 34 steps in both arms |
| Qwen3-8B (pure attn) | n-gram | 1 | ~1.01x (tie) | branching helps (+5.8%) but n-gram fires on only **28% of steps** |
| Qwen3-8B (pure attn) | EAGLE3 | 1 | **1.00x (tie)** | +17.6% acceptance on open-ended prompts, exactly cancelled by tree cost |
| Qwen3-8B | EAGLE3 | 2 / 4 / 16 | 0.98x / 0.97x / 0.96x | verification width stops being free; optimal budget 16 → 8 → 4 |
| Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ (GDN hybrid) | DFlash2, T=0 | 1 | 0.78x | structural GPU-idle bubble, below |
| same | DFlash2, default sampling | 1 | 0.69x | siblings steal spine slots; spine weaker at T=1 |
| same | DFlash2, wider trees (budget 8–32) | 1 | 0.61–0.73x | acceptance saturates at two siblings, below |

(MTP head was evaluated only as a chain baseline when choosing the production
drafter — DFlash2 dynamic-k beat it by +39.9% at concurrency 1 and tied from
8 up — never with DDT

drafter — DFlash2 dynamic-k beat it by +39.9% at concurrency 1 and tied from
8 up — never with DDTree.)

Two things the matrix says on its own. Speculation only pays on a big enough
target (0.6B: nothing beats plain decoding; 27B: chain is 2.07× base), so the
chain DDTree has to beat is strongest exactly where production runs. And the
two "bad" drafters fail for opposite reasons: n-gram is *absent* (72% of
steps have no draft to branch), DFlash2 is *too right* (rank-0 already
correct). The tree wants a drafter that is present, often wrong at rank 0,
and right at rank 1–2. EAGLE3 on open-ended prompts is the closest we found,
and it ties.

### The structural cost is GPU idle, not GPU work

Torch profiler over both arms (27B, 24 tokens, ~7.5 steps):

| | total CUDA | total CPU | wall | GPU busy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chain | 329.3 ms | 289.2 ms | 325 ms | **101%** |
| DDTree | 331.9 ms | 319.6 ms | 369 ms | **90%** |

GPU work differs by +2.6 ms; CPU by +30.4 ms. Chain speculative decoding
finishes verification entirely on the GPU — the rejection sampler is a kernel,
the CPU never intervenes — so it pipelines. A tree comes back to the CPU every
step to walk `child_maps`, and that round trip is a **4.9 ms/step bubble** at
27B. The biggest profiler entry is `cudaMemcpyAsync`, but that's the CPU
waiting on the stream, not transfer — pinned host buffers changed nothing.
Moving the walk to the GPU has a measured ceiling of 0.88x, so it still loses.

Of the original 20 ms/step gap, about half was our own integration overhead
and is gone; the numbers above are after that.

### How much acceptance is available from branching at all

We measured the ceiling rather than estimating it. A node's sampled token is
"what the target picked given that node's ancestor context", which stays valid
in **any sub-tree containing that node** — so one wide tree run with tracing
gives acceptance for every sub-shape offline. We also log the drafter's top-16
per depth, so sibling hit rates come out unbiased.

27B + DFlash2, 6 open-ended prompts × 192 tokens, batch 1, greedy:

| shape | tokens/step | steps |
|---|---|---|

content.content:
**Paper:** arXiv:2404.19124v2, dated 06 Jun 2024, by Davis Wertheimer, Joshua Rosenkranz, Thomas Parnell, Sahil Suneja, Pavithra Ranganathan, Raghu Ganti and Mudhakar Srivatsa (IBM Research).

**1. Does it build candidate trees from per-head top-k?**
Yes. Each stage branches on its most likely tokens, and the resulting tree is pruned to k candidates.
- "The model thus emits an entire tree of candidates"
- The user can "select the top-k most likely predictions from that tree"
- For Llama2-7B: "a tree with 6 branches at the first head, 3 at the second, and 2 at the third"
- "we prune this tree of 6∗3∗2=36 candidates down to the desired k base on confidence"
- The k candidates are checked in parallel using "multi-candidate decoding [9] and Tree Attention"

**2. Does it adjust the number of candidates based on batch size?**
Partly. It uses a coarse on/off approach rather than fine-grained tuning.
- The paper suggests "fixing k=1, trading off a slightly higher latency for b<4 for much better behavior at b>4"
- "we can also disable speculative decoding dynamically for b above a given threshold, such as 32"
- Truly adaptive tuning is left as future work: "we'd like to swap dynamically to the optimal value for each incoming inference request"
- That would replace "simply toggling on/off between default values of k=(0,1,5)"

**3. Does it adjust speculation length based on batch size?**
No. The number of heads is fixed for each model: 3 for the Llama2 models, 7 for Codellama and 5 for Granite-20B. Head count was chosen by data domain (code is more predictable) and by training memory limits, not by batch size.

I found the paper. On your "tree" keyword: none of the sources say DEER uses tree-structured drafting or verification. It checks one straight block of draft tokens. The closest tree-based work in the results is a later paper called DART.

**The paper**
- **arXiv:** 2512.15176, submitted 17 Dec 2025. Authors: Zicong Cheng, Guo-Wei Yang, Jia Li, Zhijie Deng, Meng-Hao Guo, Shi-Min Hu
- **Category:** cs.LG
- **Project page:** https://czc726.github.io/DEER/

**The problem it addresses**
In speculative decoding, a small "drafter" model guesses several tokens ahead and the large target model checks them. The authors say the usual approach, an autoregressive drafter that writes one token at a time, has two problems: (1) step-wise uncertainty accumulation leads to a progressive collapse of trust between the target model and the drafter, and (2) inherently sequential decoding of AR drafters. DEER is an efficient speculative decoding framework that drafts with diffusion and verifies with AR models.

**How it works**
- **Training:** DEER employs a two-stage training pipeline to align the dLLM-based drafters with the target AR model, and further adopts single-step decoding to generate long draft segments. In Stage II, the model is trained to mask only the last R tokens of the answer rather than the full suffix, and it appl[ies] exponentially decaying weights, giving higher emphasis to tokens right after the prefix.
- **Inference (block-based, not a tree):** given a prefix x1:j, the dLLM proposes a block of k draft tokens in parallel. The AR verifier then walks through the block position by position: Compute the acceptance probability from the ratio between AR and draft distributions. Rejected tokens are resampled from a residual distribution, which guarantees that DEER is a lossless decoding scheme, producing the exact same output distribution as direct sampling from the target AR model.
- **Why errors don't snowball:** All candidate tokens in a block are predicted jointly from the same prefix, instead of being chained autoregressively.

**Results**
- Experiments show DEER reaches draft acceptance lengths of up to 32 tokens, far surpassing the 10 tokens achieved by EAGLE-3. (32 is the maximum; the average is lower, see the next point.)
- On HumanEval with Qwen3-30B-A3B, DEER achieves a 5.54x speedup compared to EAGLE-3's 2.41x, and an average acceptance length of 5.03 tokens versus EAGLE-3's 3.05 tokens.
- It also scales to batches, yielding substantial speedups (e.g., nearly 4× at batch size 8 on HumanEval) even without full KV-cache integration for dLLMs.
- The authors call it the first speculative decoding framework that relies exclusively on a discrete-space dLLM as the drafter. They also report a new ability they call "reliable block regeneration," wherein the dLLM can perform genuinely blockwise generation from incrementally masked suffixes.
- **Limitations (from a third-party review):** current implementations face challenges regarding KV cache integration in standard inference frameworks and training complexity.

**Related tree-based work: DART (arXiv 2601.19278, Jan 2026)**
DART cites DEER and takes a different route. DART predicts logits for multiple future masked positions in parallel within a single forward pass based on hidden states of the target model, and it adds an efficient tree pruning algorithm that constructs high-quality draft token trees with N-gram–enforced semantic continuity. It also argues that directly adopting diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) as draft models (Christopher et al., 2025; Sandler et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025) suffers from fundamental limitations. The Cheng et al. citation there refers to DEER.

content.content:
**Source:** *Optimizing Speculative Decoding for Serving Large Language Models Using Goodput* (arXiv:2406.14066v2, 25 Jun 2024), by Xiaoxuan Liu, Cade Daniel, Langxiang Hu, Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Xiangxi Mo, Alvin Cheung, Zhijie Deng, Ion Stoica and Hao Zhang (UC Berkeley, Anyscale, UCSD, SJTU).

The page describes **SmartSpec** only. "TurboSpec" does not appear anywhere in it.

**Does it handle tree-style/Medusa decoding?** Yes, but only in simulation.
- "Prior to integrating SmartSpec, Medusa could only be implemented with a batch size of 1."
- "we simulate Medusa with continuous batching and assess its performance both with and without SmartSpec integration"
- The authors used a simulator partly because "devising an effective verification kernel for tree-structured speculative decoding proves difficult."

**How tree size is chosen**
- "For Top-k tree-style speculative decoding, SmartSpec will identify the optimal Top-k value for each proposal head."
- They "evaluate performance using goodput to decide the number of sampled tokens per head."
- Goodput is generated tokens per second of execution time.
- Expected accepted length comes from per-head acceptance rates, assumed independent and tracked with a moving average.
- Cost comes from a profiled linear latency model. With full trees, the tokens verified per request equal the sum of cumulative products of each head's top-k.
- SmartSpec builds candidate batches from first-come-first-served prefixes. For each, it picks the settings with the highest goodput, then keeps the best batch.

**How the token budget adapts to load**
- "As batch size increases, the optimal proposal length decreases."
- "under extremely high system loads, goodput would automatically turn off speculation"
- Fixed trees struggle under load: "fixed top2/top3 Medusa quickly explode the batch size." For example, choosing 3, 2 and 2 tokens per head adds 21 verification tokens, even though at most 4 tokens can be accepted.
- With SmartSpec, "In both scenarios (α is 0.6 or 0.8), SmartSpec quickly reverts to top-1 sampling." This leaves about 4 batched tokens per request.
- "SmartSpec effectively maintains manageable request latencies even under high request rates."

I couldn't find an arXiv paper called "TreeDiff" about speculative decoding. A paper by that name does exist, but it covers a different topic. Several other recent papers do combine diffusion drafters with draft trees, and one of them may be what you're after.

**What "TreeDiff" actually is (arXiv 2508.01473)**
The paper is "TreeDiff: AST-Guided Code Generation with Diffusion LLMs." It presents a syntax-aware diffusion framework that incorporates structural priors from Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) into the corruption process. TreeDiff moves beyond uniform random masking by selectively targeting syntactically critical elements. In other words, it's about training diffusion models to write code, not about speeding up decoding.

**Papers on diffusion plus draft trees for speculative decoding**

1. **DDTree, "Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Block Diffusion Draft Trees" (arXiv 2604.12989, April 2026, Ringel & Romano).** This may be the paper you mean. It starts from DFlash, which shows that a block diffusion drafter can generate an entire draft block in a single forward pass. However, vanilla DFlash still verifies only a single drafted trajectory per round, potentially limiting its acceptance length. DDTree constructs a draft tree directly from the per-position distributions of a block diffusion drafter. Under a fixed node budget, DDTree uses a simple best-first heap algorithm to choose candidates, and the resulting tree is verified efficiently in a single target model forward pass using an ancestor-only attention mask.

2. **DARTree, "Speculative Diffusion Decoding with Autoregressive Draft Trees" (arXiv 2608.13524, August 2026).** It is a training-free speculative decoding method that extends a pretrained AR correction head from chains to trees. The authors report accepting up to 12.97 tokens per verification round, 98.6% more than DFlash and 27.9% more than Domino in the same setting, and reaching up to 9.73× lossless speedup.

3. **BASTION (arXiv 2605.29727, May 2026).** A budget-aware speculative decoding method with tree-based diffusion drafting. Unlike existing methods that rely on static tree topologies, Bastion dynamically constructs query-dependent trees by balancing draft quality against hardware constraints.

4. **TreeFlash, "Parallel AR-Approximation for Faster Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2606.03819).** Another tree-based method built on DFlash-style one-shot block drafting.

5. **Earlier related work:**
   - SpecDiff ("Speculative Diffusion Decoding," arXiv 2408.05636) proposes to replace the auto-regressive drafter with recently introduced discrete diffusion models.
   - DART (arXiv 2601.19278) is a very recent work that also constructs draft trees from one-pass parallel logits.

If you had a particular paper in mind, any extra detail you have would help pin it down, such as an author, the year, or a key result. My best guess is DDTree.

When Parallel Drafter Meets Parallel Speculative Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.27396"},{"title":"\\scalerel* Exploring and Improving Drafts in Blockwise Parallel Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2404.09221v2"},{"title":"Exploring and Improving Drafts in Blockwise Parallel Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2404.09221"},{"title":"Speculative Speculative Decoding Tanishq Kumar1,* Tri Dao2,3 Avner May3","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03251"},{"title":"ParallelSpec: Parallel Drafter for Efficient Speculative Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05589v1"},{"title":"[2609.27396v1] When Parallel Drafter Meets Parallel Speculative Decoding","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27396v1"},{"title":"LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding · Pith","url":"https://pith.science/paper/2608.20530"},{"title":"Efficient speculative decoding with a fixed-cost parallel drafter","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2609.37029v1"}]

I found several relevant papers. None is called "lattice speculative decoding" exactly, but these cover the ideas in your query: candidate lattices from block drafters, parallel drafting and parallel draft/verify.

**1. LiLiCorr (arXiv 2608.20530, submitted Aug 2026). This is the closest match to "token lattice + block drafter."**
- Its main claim is that the incoherence of parallel block drafters can be fixed at draft time without extra target passes or per-slot networks.
- How it works: LiLiCorr keeps the top-K tokens each draft slot proposes, runs one lightweight Transformer over the whole candidate lattice, and scores each adjacent pair by the cosine similarity of a learned out vector and in vector. Then a greedy left-to-right argmax walk, which touches no network weights, commits the final block.
- Results: over the vanilla DFlash drafter, LiLiCorr raises acceptance length on every benchmark by 9 to 19%, while its scoring head accounts for about 2.8% of the per-block latency.
- Limitation: the method relies on the coverage assumption that the correct token is present in the top-K pool, with K (candidates per slot) = 8.

**2. DPara: "When Parallel Drafter Meets Parallel Speculative Decoding" (arXiv 2609.27396, Sep 23, 2026)**
- The problem it addresses: DSpark-style parallel drafters have made speculative decoding highly effective, yet their draft phase remains serialized on the critical path of every round.
- Method: while the target verifies, DPara's diffusion backbone precomputes draft representations for every acceptance boundary with the bonus left unspecified; a lightweight autoregressive head then combines the revealed verification outcome with the matching precomputed representation to produce the next draft.
- Results: on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B across seven math, coding, and chat benchmarks, DPara achieves average speedups of 3.21× and 3.52× over autoregressive decoding.
- It also measures how often SSD has to fall back to serial drafting: at batch size 16, up to 96% of steps fall back.

**3. Speculative Speculative Decoding (SSD), by Kumar, Dao and May (arXiv 2603.03251)**
- In SSD the draft model predicts what verification outcomes are most likely, and prepares (i.e., pre-speculates) for all of them in parallel to the verification taking place.
- Unlike tree methods, it scales up the speculation compute by pre-speculating for many verification outcomes in parallel, but does not introduce any additional verifier compute.

**4. Fixed-cost parallel drafter (arXiv 2609.37029, about a week old)**
- It targets drafting cost that grows with context length. As the authors put it, as the context grows, existing state-of-the-art drafters become increasingly expensive, eroding the very efficiency advantage they are designed to provide.
- For future work it suggests that exploring tree-structured and multi-drafter verification schemes could help increase the number of accepted tokens per round.

**5. Older background: "Exploring and Improving Drafts in Blockwise Parallel Decoding" (arXiv 2404.09221, 2024)**
- This is the origin of the "top-k lattice" idea for block drafters. In this lattice, any path from the start to final state represents a viable draft. It rescores the lattice with neural or n-gram language models.
- They show that lattice rescoring can improve the block efficiency for a 1.5 billion parameter blockwise parallel LM. One drawback is memory: running many candidate drafts with lattice rescoring can introduce high demands on memory.

**6. ParallelSpec (arXiv 2410.05589, 2024)**
- An earlier parallel drafter. At each draft step, the drafter generates k tokens with a single forward pass, and then they are sent to the target model for parallel verification.

I didn't find a 2026 paper that explicitly combines beam search over a block drafter's lattice with lattice-structured verification. LiLiCorr (lattice reranking) and the 2024 BPD rescoring paper come closest.

LiLiCorr is an NVIDIA method that sits on top of DFlash's parallel drafts. It reranks the drafted tokens so they fit together better, and vLLM supports it starting with v0.31.0.

## The problem it solves
DFlash is a speculative decoding method that uses a small diffusion-LLM draft model to predict an entire block of tokens in a single forward pass, conditioned on hidden states from the target model. The drawback is that it is trained on the per-position marginals rather than on the joint distribution over the block, so the tokens it emits are individually plausible yet jointly incoherent. In other words, each token is predicted on its own, so neighboring tokens may not make sense together.

## How LiLiCorr works
- The name stands for a Lightweight Likelihood-based model that Correlates the per-position marginals such a drafter produces.
- It keeps the top-K tokens at each position and processes them jointly, emitting an in and an out vector for each. Two candidates at consecutive positions match when the earlier out vector aligns, in cosine similarity, with the later in vector.
- One network pass produces every vector, the pairwise scores are a single batched matmul, and only the greedy walk stays sequential. Verify is untouched, so outputs remain distributionally identical to the target model's — only acceptance length and throughput change.
- Related methods Domino and DSpark take a different approach: they reintroduce a sequential dependency between positions by running a correction network once at every position.

## Reported results (arXiv 2608.20530, NVIDIA)
- The current version (v2) says that it raises acceptance length by 7 to 19%, while its single-pass scoring head costs only about 3% of the per-block latency. Compared with three methods developed at the same time, LiLiCorr holds the highest throughput in 63 of those settings, ties within a measured noise floor in 6, and trails in only 3.
- Version 1 reported somewhat different numbers: a 9–19% gain and the highest throughput in 70 of 72 settings, measured against two rival methods instead of three.
- Built-in limit: LiLiCorr reranks only the top-K tokens the drafter proposes, so a slot whose correct token is absent from that pool cannot be recovered.

## vLLM docs and usage
- vLLM v0.31.0 added it: the release notes list the LiLiCorr drafter (#57934).
- From the vLLM docs page: LiLiCorr uses a DFlash backbone to produce per-position candidates, then scores candidate combinations with a learned correlator. It requires a compatible trained checkpoint and Model Runner V2, which is selected automatically. Both plain and grouped-convolution checkpoints are supported.
- Example command from the docs:
  ```
  vllm serve /path/to/target --dtype bfloat16 \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/path/to/lilicorr","num_speculative_tokens":15,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
  ```
  The docs strongly recommend explicitly setting num_speculative_tokens to the checkpoint's trained block_size - 1 (for example, 15 for block_size=16). The trained block includes one anchor position.
- Checkpoint requirements: The checkpoint must declare LiLiCorrDraftModel and include all lilicorr_* geometry fields and trained head weights. Geometry is read from dflash_config.
- There is also an open pull request to bring it to vLLM-Ascend (Huawei NPUs), and its documentation stresses the requirement for eager execution mode.

**Other sources:** the NVIDIA project page is research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/lilicorr/. One independent review points out that no code or checkpoints are released with the paper. However, a ModelOpt pull request fixing LiLiCorr exports for vLLM suggests NVIDIA's tooling can produce compatible checkpoints.

- One network pass produces every vector, the pairwise scores are a single batched matmul, and only the greedy walk stays sequential. Verify is untouched, so outputs remain distributionally identical to the target model's — only acceptance length and throughput change.
- Related methods Domino and DSpark take a different approach: they reintroduce a sequential dependency between positions by running a correction network once at every position.

## Reported results (arXiv 2608.20530, NVIDIA)
- The current version (v2) says that it raises acceptance length by 7 to 19%, while its single-pass scoring head costs only about 3% of the per-block latency. Compared with three methods developed at the same time, LiLiCorr holds the highest throughput in 63 of those settings, ties within a measured noise floor in 6, and trails in only 3.
- Version 1 reported somewhat different numbers: a 9–19% gain and the highest throughput in 70 of 72 settings, measured against two rival methods instead of three.
- Built-in limit: LiLiCorr reranks only the top-K tokens the drafter proposes, so a slot whose correct token is absent from that pool cannot be recovered.

## vLLM docs and usage
- vLLM v0.31.0 added it: the release notes list the LiLiCorr drafter (#57934).
- From the vLLM docs page: LiLiCorr uses a DFlash backbone to produce per-position candidates, then scores candidate combinations with a learned correlator. It requires a compatible trained checkpoint and Model Runner V2, which is selected automatically. Both plain and grouped-convolution checkpoints are supported.
- Example command from the docs:
  ```
  vllm serve /path/to/target --dtype bfloat16 \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/path/to/lilicorr","num_speculative_tokens":15,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
  ```
  The docs strongly recommend explicitly setting num_speculative_tokens to the checkpoint's trained block_size - 1 (for example, 15 for block_size=16). The trained block includes one anchor position.
- Checkpoint requirements: The checkpoint must declare LiLiCorrDraftModel and include all lilicorr_* geometry fields and trained head weights. Geometry is read from dflash_config.
- There is also an open pull request to bring it to vLLM-Ascend (Huawei NPUs), and its documentation stresses the requirement for eager execution mode.

**Other sources:** the NVIDIA project page is research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/lilicorr/. One independent review points out that no code or checkpoints are released with the paper. However, a ModelOpt pull request fixing LiLiCorr exports for vLLM suggests NVIDIA's tooling can produce compatible checkpoints.

# Project image: official vLLM ROCm release (built for gfx90a/MI250) + experiment tooling.
# Bump VLLM_TAG to upgrade vLLM; check `strings _C.abi3.so | grep gfx90a` after each bump.
ARG VLLM_TAG=v0.30.0
FROM vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:${VLLM_TAG}

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir pandas matplotlib seaborn jsonlines arctic-inference==0.3.0

# gfx90a workaround: wvSplitK skinny GEMM is 2.4x/5.7x slower than hipBLASLt at 3/5 tokens
# (see scripts/gemm_latency.py), which cripples spec-decode verify (1 + 4 draft = 5 tokens)
# and any 3/5-request decode batch. Keep it only where it wins (1, 2, 4 tokens).
RUN f=$(python3 -c "import vllm, os; print(os.path.dirname(vllm.__file__))")/model_executor/layers/utils.py \
 && grep -q "if m > 8 and 0 < n <= 5:" "$f" \
 && sed -i 's/if m > 8 and 0 < n <= 5:/if m > 8 and n in (1, 2, 4):  # lossless-dec gfx90a patch/' "$f"

ENV HF_HOME=/models/hf \
    VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn

WORKDIR /workspace
ENTRYPOINT []
CMD ["bash"]

COPY patch_pixtral.py /tmp/patch_pixtral.py
RUN python3 /tmp/patch_pixtral.py

COPY patch_eagle_mistral.py /tmp/patch_eagle_mistral.py

input.message:
## Bottom line
Both halves of the idea are already published. DDTree (Apr 2026) builds a budgeted best-first token tree from DFlash's one-pass marginals and verifies it with an ancestor-only mask in one target pass. Earlier, Medusa, ParallelSpec and 2502.05947 did the same thing with parallel heads. The load-adaptive version came out 29 Sep 2026 as CAST: cost-aware tree width from a profiled verify-latency slope, plus one verifier budget shared best-first across concurrent requests. TreeSpark does something similar with a tree-growth price indexed by batch size. For chains, DSpark and vLLM's Adaptive Verification already do batch-global budgeting against a profiled cost curve. No vLLM release has ever supported tree verification for a parallel drafter, tree attention was removed in v0.21, and it never ran on ROCm.

## 1. Trees or multi-draft built from parallel/diffusion per-position marginals
**Identical**
- **DDTree**, "Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Block Diffusion Draft Trees" — [2604.12989](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12989) (Apr 2026). The project page lists it as a preprint; one later paper cites it as COLM 2026.
  - Method: one DFlash pass, then top-B prefixes ranked by the product of marginals via a best-first heap. This is provably optimal for the factorized draft surrogate.
  - Verification: ancestor-only mask, one target pass. Losslessness comes from walking the tree with the target's own sampling rule.
  - Setup: HF Transformers with SDPA, effectively batch 1, budgets swept 16–1024 with the best at 256–512. Beats DFlash in 60/60 settings (Qwen3-8B MATH-500: 5.56x to 7.52x).
  - No load adaptation.
- **CAST**, "Cost-Aware Speculative Trees from One-Pass Block Drafters" — [2610.00321](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00321) (v1 29 Sep 2026). Closest to your full idea.
  - Drafters: DFlash and DART trees, built best-first from marginals.
  - Width rule: keep adding nodes while prefix mass ≥ current throughput × per-node verify cost. The cost slope is profiled per GPU.
  - Concurrency: one shared verifier budget, allocated best-first across B requests. The best static width shrinks to a chain by B≥16. Adaptive allocation gives +7–14% goodput over the best static width at B=16/32.
  - Lossless at T>0 via recursive rejection sampling without replacement.
  - Limits: custom harness, NVIDIA only (no vLLM, no ROCm), decode-only timing.
- **Same algorithm on older drafters:**
  - "Acceleration Multiple Heads Decoding via Dynamic Tree Attention" [2502.05947](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05947) (Feb 2025): DDTree's top-n-by-product-of-marginals priority queue, applied to Medusa heads.
